title: Carboxylic acids
learningObjective: know that carboxylic acids contain the functional group; understand how to draw structural and displayed formulae for unbranched-chain carboxylic acids with up to four carbon atoms in the molecule, and name each compound; describe the reactions of aqueous solutions of carboxylic acids with metals and metal carbonates; know that vinegar is an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid

sections.title: Carboxylic acids
sections.markdown:
The alcohols lesson ended with a sour note: oxidise ethanol —
microbially in open air or sharply in the lab with dichromate(VI)
— and the product is **ethanoic acid**. That product is not a
one-off. It is the representative of a whole family of organic
acids, the **[[carboxylic-acid]]s**, and this lesson gives that
family the same treatment the alcohols received: structure first,
then names, then reactions (u4:c26).

Every member of the family carries the same [[functional-group]]:
the **carboxyl group, –COOH**. Read the arrangement carefully,
because it is two groups welded onto one carbon — a carbonyl
(C=O) and a hydroxyl (O–H) sharing the same end carbon atom:

```
      O
      ‖
—C—O—H
```

That shared carbon is what makes the chemistry of this family
different from both the alcohols (O–H alone) and the aldehydes
(C=O alone). It is also why the group is always found at the end
of a chain: the bonding arrangement needs a carbon with a spare
bond for the rest of the molecule.

The most familiar member is [[ethanoic-acid]], which carried the
old name *acetic acid* — and the everyday face of the family is
**[[vinegar]]**: an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid
(4.37C). The sour taste of vinegar and the sharpness of the
family are the same chemistry at different dilutions.

The family is built by oxidation. A carboxylic acid forms when
its corresponding alcohol is oxidised — leave ethanol exposed to
air and its resident microorganisms, or oxidise it deliberately
with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid, and the
–OH-bearing carbon climbs one rung up the oxidation ladder to
–COOH (Sections 4–5 of the alcohols lesson). The rung above it
on that ladder does not exist at IGCSE: the carboxylic acids
are where the oxidation story of the alcohols stops.

:::prior-knowledge
Before this lesson you should be fluent with three ideas from
the alcohols lesson (u4:c26): the –OH functional group and how
it is drawn; the two oxidation routes to ethanoic acid — microbial
(slow, in the air) and laboratory (dichromate(VI), orange to
green); and the naming habit of counting carbons in the chain.
If any of those wobble, repair them first — this family is the
alcohols' oxidation product, and every name here is the alcohol
name with its ending swapped.
:::

:::did-you-know
The family's one-carbon member, methanoic acid, is old enough to
have its own delivery system: the sting of a stinging nettle is
a dose of a dilute methanoic-acid solution injected through the
plant's hollow hairs. The traditional remedy — rubbing a leaf of
the dock plant that tends to grow nearby — is folk chemistry,
but the acid in the sting is this lesson's smallest acid.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Vinegar is economics and history in a bottle. Before
refrigeration, the acetic acid in vinegar was the world's main
food preservative — pickling works because bacteria cannot
survive the low pH, so harvests survived winters. Different
civilisations fermented whatever they grew: wine into wine
vinegar, malt into malt vinegar, rice into rice vinegar. One
molecule — ethanoic acid — supporting food security across
every grain-growing culture on Earth.
:::

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.34C says *know* the functional group — this is a
recall item, not a derivation. Reproduce the arrangement from
memory: carbonyl C=O **and** hydroxyl O–H on the same carbon,
written –COOH. The classic lost mark is writing –OH and calling
it the carboxylic-acid group; that is the alcohol group. The
carboxyl group has the double-bonded oxygen, and drawing or
writing it earns the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Ethanoic acid contains –OH, so it is an alcohol." The hydroxyl
part of –COOH is bonded to a carbon that also carries the C=O —
and that second oxygen changes the family, the name and the
reactions entirely. Functional groups are judged by their whole
arrangement, not by spotting one fragment inside them. The same
O–H appears in both families; the C=O is what makes this one
an acid.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write and draw the carboxyl group –COOH with both bonds
explicit? Can you name the family's everyday representative and
state what vinegar is a solution of (4.37C)? Can you say which
oxidation routes build the family from alcohols? If yes, the
structure of this lesson is loaded and the naming section is
next.
:::

sections.title: Drawing and naming the carboxylic acids
sections.markdown:
Statement 4.35C narrows the task to the four simplest members of
the [[homologous-series]] — [[methanoic-acid]], ethanoic,
propanoic and butanoic acid — and asks for the three levels of
formula plus the name of each. The naming engine is the same one the alkanes,
alkenes and alcohols used: meth- means one carbon, eth- two,
prop- three, but- four, and the acid ending *-anoic acid* replaces
the alcohol's *-anol*.

| acid | molecular formula | structural formula |
|------|-------------------|--------------------|
| methanoic acid | CH₂O₂ | HCOOH |
| ethanoic acid | C₂H₄O₂ | CH₃COOH |
| propanoic acid | C₃H₆O₂ | CH₃CH₂COOH |
| butanoic acid | C₄H₈O₂ | CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH |

The [[molecular-formula]] counts each element's atoms; the
[[structural-formula]] shows the order of the atoms unambiguously
— every member ends in COOH with the hydrogen-bearing chain
before it. The molecular formulae share the pattern CnH2nO2:
each member is its corresponding alcohol with one extra oxygen
atom — the oxidation that builds the carboxyl group. Methanol
CH₄O oxidised gives methanoic acid CH₂O₂; ethanol C₂H₆O gives
ethanoic acid C₂H₄O₂. The carbon count never changes on the way
up.

The [[displayed-formula]] level is where the discipline lives.
Every bond must be drawn — the chain as C–C and C–H lines, and
the carboxyl end with the C=O double bond and the O–H single
bond shown explicitly. Methanoic acid's displayed formula is
H–C(=O)–O–H with both bonds on the same carbon visible. The
condensed COOH is a convenience for equations; the drawn-out
arrangement is what *displayed* means.

:::key-point
When naming a carboxylic acid, count the **total** number of
carbon atoms — including the one inside the –COOH group. Propanoic
acid has three carbons in total, which is why it starts with
*prop*: the two chain carbons plus the carboxyl carbon. Because
the –COOH group is always on the end carbon, there is no need
to insert a number into the name to locate the functional group
— no locant exists anywhere in this family.
:::

:::exam-hint
If an item asks for a displayed formula, draw all the bonding in
the COOH group — the C=O and the O–H both explicit. If an item
asks for the formula inside an *equation*, the condensed form is
normal and correct: CH₃COOH. Reading the demand curve of the
question — drawing item versus equation item — tells you which
level to produce, and mixing them up is the standard lost mark
here.
:::

:::did-you-know
The old name of ethanoic acid, *acetic*, comes from *acetum*,
Latin for vinegar — the Romans named the family's famous member
after its most famous solution. The name survives in English
words like *acetate* (the ethanoate ion's old name) and in
*nail-varnish remover*, whose solvent was once called acetone
for the same reasons.
:::

:::misconception
"Butanoic acid has four carbons in its chain." No — butanoic
acid has four carbons **in total**, three in the chain plus the
carboxyl carbon. Students who count only the CH₃CH₂CH₂– part
write butanoic acid as having three carbons and then mis-draw
the formula. The carboxyl carbon is a real carbon atom: it sits
in the count, it sits in the molecular formula (the C of COOH),
and it sits in the displayed drawing with its C=O bond.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write molecular, structural and displayed formulae for
all four members up to four carbons, with the COOH end drawn
out? Can you explain why propanoic acid carries *prop* and why
no locant number is ever needed? Can you state how many carbons
each molecular formula's n counts? Three yeses and 4.35C is
banked.
:::

sections.title: Acid properties of the carboxylic acids
sections.markdown:
Ethanoic acid and the other carboxylic acids are **[[weak-acid]]s**
— a label this section uses and Section 5 finally explains. In
practical terms: their solutions have a pH of about 3–5 (the
exact value depends on the concentration), they turn blue litmus
paper red, and they react with everything you expect an acid to
react with. Weak does not mean inactive — the family passes every
classical test of an acid; it just runs the reactions more
gently than hydrochloric or sulfuric acid do.

Everything that follows takes [[ethanoic-acid]] as the worked
example, because it is the member you are most likely to meet in
a laboratory or a kitchen. The other members behave the same way:
if a question switches the acid, all you change is the formula —
CH₃COOH becomes CH₃CH₂COOH, and the reaction writing itself is
unchanged. That is the practical payoff of a homologous series:
learn one member's reactions, own the family's.

Two reaction families deliver Statement 4.36C, and each gets its
own section: the reaction with **metals** (next section, salts
plus hydrogen) and the reaction with **metal carbonates** (the
section after, salts plus carbon dioxide plus water). Both are
re-runs of acid chemistry met in Unit 2 — what is new here is
only the acid, and the ethanoate salts it leaves behind.

:::exam-hint
"State two ways ethanoic acid behaves like other acids" is a
gift item if you keep the acid-test checklist ready: turns blue
litmus red, pH below 7 (about 3–5 here), reacts with metals
above hydrogen, reacts with carbonates giving carbon dioxide.
Any two score. The trap is overclaiming — the family is weak,
so "reacts violently" or "pH about 1" statements contradict the
chemistry and cost the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"A weak acid is a harmless acid." Weak describes how far the
acid ionises in water, not how safe it is. Ethanoic acid still
turns litmus red, still fizzes with carbonates, and concentrated
solutions are corrosive. What weak actually changes is the
*rate and extent* of those reactions — Section 5 gives the
dissociation picture behind the word.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the pH band of the family, the litmus result, and
the two reaction families that deliver 4.36C? Can you explain
why learning ethanoic acid's reactions effectively teaches the
whole family? Can you say what "weak" does and does not mean
yet? Then the metals are waiting.
:::

sections.title: Reaction with metals
sections.markdown:
The Unit 2 rule still stands: a metal above hydrogen in the
[[reactivity-series]] reacts with a dilute acid to give a
[[salt]] and hydrogen (u2:c14, u2:c16). Dilute ethanoic acid
obeys it exactly as hydrochloric acid does — only more slowly,
which is the [[weak-acid]] behaviour of the last section showing
through. The new thing is not the reaction type; it is the salt,
because every carboxylic acid has its own family of salts built
on the **ethanoate** ion.

Drop magnesium ribbon into dilute ethanoic acid and it fizzes
vigorously: hydrogen gas streams off and the solid disappears
into a colourless solution of **magnesium ethanoate**:

Mg(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → (CH₃COO)₂Mg(aq) + H₂(g)

That formula deserves a slow read, because the salt formulae are
where students reliably stumble. Magnesium ethanoate is an
[[ionic-compound]]: it contains magnesium ions, Mg²⁺, and
ethanoate ions, CH₃COO⁻. Each [[ethanoate-ion]] carries a single
negative charge, so a doubly-charged magnesium ion needs **two**
of them to balance the charges — hence the subscript 2 and hence
the 2 in front of the acid in the equation. The metal is written
after the ethanoate groups because that order reflects the
structure: the positive magnesium ion is attracted to the
negative charge sitting on the oxygen atoms of the ethanoate
ions.

The ethanoate ion itself is worth a picture in words: a
CH₃–C(=O) unit with the spare oxygen carrying the negative
charge — written CH₃COO⁻. It is the carboxylic-acid molecule
with its acidic hydrogen removed; the O–H proton is what the
metal takes away, and the electron it leaves behind becomes the
ion's charge. Draw it as the carboxyl group minus one H, with
a minus sign on the single-bonded oxygen.

Other metals behave exactly as the reactivity-series predicts.
Sodium is dangerously reactive with the acid — do not try it
outside a demonstration. Zinc produces bubbles of hydrogen
noticeably more slowly than it does with hydrochloric acid, a
direct visual of the weak-acid speed difference. Metals below
hydrogen in the series — copper, silver — do not react at all.
Wherever a reaction does take place, a metal ethanoate forms
alongside the hydrogen: zinc ethanoate is (CH₃COO)₂Zn, built by
the same two-ethanoates-per-ion arithmetic.

:::key-point
Every metal-ethanoate formula is a charge-balance exercise, and
the ethanoate ion is always 1−. So the metal's ion charge sets
the subscript: Mg²⁺ takes two ethanoates, (CH₃COO)₂Mg; Na⁺ takes
one, CH₃COONa; Al³⁺ takes three, (CH₃COO)₃Al. Work the charges
first and the formula writes itself — never balance metal
ethanoates by trial and error.
:::

:::exam-hint
Salt-formula items are marked on the ion arithmetic, so show it:
Mg²⁺ + 2CH₃COO⁻ → (CH₃COO)₂Mg. The equation mark for
2CH₃COOH(aq) in front of the arrow is earned by the same
arithmetic — two acid molecules donate two protons to build the
two ethanoate ions. State symbols complete the mark: (s), (aq),
(g) as in the magnesium equation above.
:::

:::misconception
"Ethanoic acid plus magnesium gives CH₃COOMg." That formula
balances nothing — one 1− ion cannot neutralise one 2+ ion. The
error is forgetting that the ethanoate ion is a single-charge
unit; the fix is writing the two ions first and subscripting
after. The same discipline separates zinc ethanoate
((CH₃COO)₂Zn, correct) from ZnCOO (not a formula at all).
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the magnesium-plus-ethanoic equation with state
symbols and explain where the 2s come from? Can you build the
formula of sodium ethanoate, zinc ethanoate and magnesium
ethanoate from ion charges? Can you predict what copper does in
dilute ethanoic acid and why? Charges first, formula second —
and this section is yours.
:::

sections.title: Weak and strong acids
sections.markdown:
This section is the *why* behind the [[weak-acid]] label — it runs
one step beyond the statement list, which is exactly why the
family's acid behaviour has been described so far only in
outcomes. The distinction is about **[[dissociation]]**: how
completely an acid splits into ions when it dissolves in water.

Ethanoic acid is a weak acid. The acids met earlier in the
course — hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid — are **[[strong-acid]]s**.
The word measures ionisation, and nothing else. A strong acid
dissociates completely in water: a solution of hydrochloric acid
contains mostly H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions and hardly any intact HCl
molecules at all. A weak acid dissociates only partially: for
ethanoic acid, only about 1 molecule in every 75 splits into H⁺
and CH₃COO⁻ — the rest stay whole, sitting in the solution
dissolved but not ionised.

That single sentence explains every observation in this chapter.
Same concentration of ethanoic acid and hydrochloric acid: the
ethanoic solution holds far fewer H⁺ ions per litre, so it reacts
with metals or metal carbonates much more slowly (fewer protons
available to collide per second), and its pH sits higher. The
acid still reacts — the reactions are just protracted, because
each dissociated H⁺ that reacts nudges the equilibrium of the
remaining molecules to dissociate a little more. Weak acids do
the whole of an acid's job; they do it at a lower H⁺ concentration.

:::key-point
Strength and concentration are independent variables. Strength
(dissociation: completely vs partially into ions) is about the
molecules themselves; concentration (dilute vs concentrated) is
about how much acid is dissolved per unit volume. A dilute
solution of a strong acid and a concentrated solution of a weak
acid can hold similar H⁺ concentrations — the words cross-cut,
and conflating them is the single most common misconception in
acids chemistry.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why ethanoic acid reacts more slowly with magnesium
than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration" is a two-mark
classic. Mark 1: ethanoic acid is weak / partially dissociated /
only about 1 in 75 molecules ionise. Mark 2: so the H⁺(aq)
concentration is lower / fewer hydrogen ions per unit volume.
Answers through concentration ("it is more dilute") score nothing
— the question fixes the concentration identical; the answer
must route through dissociation.
:::

:::misconception
"Strong acids are concentrated acids, weak acids are dilute
acids." Whether an acid is strong or weak has nothing to do with
its concentration. Concentrated hydrochloric acid and dilute
hydrochloric acid are both strong acids — both dissociate
completely; they differ only in how much of them is dissolved.
Concentrated ethanoic acid (glacial acetic acid) is still a weak
acid — still only partially ionised, whatever its concentration.
Four combinations exist, and every one of them is real.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define the strong/weak distinction through dissociation
and quote the 1-in-75 picture for ethanoic acid? Can you explain
the slower reaction rate through H⁺ concentration? Can you pair
the four combinations (strong/weak × concentrated/dilute) with a
real example of each? Then the label "weak" is fully earned and
the carbonates are next.
:::

sections.title: Reaction with carbonates
sections.markdown:
The second reaction family of Statement 4.36C is the carbonates:
a [[metal-carbonate]] reacts with an acid to give a [[salt]],
carbon dioxide and water — the Unit 2 rule again (u2:c16), and
dilute ethanoic acid obeys it like any other acid. What changes
is only the salt, and the same ethanoate arithmetic as the
metals section runs underneath it.

With sodium carbonate the reaction fizzes vigorously and leaves
a colourless solution of **sodium ethanoate**:

Na₂CO₃(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → 2CH₃COONa(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

With calcium carbonate the story repeats: lots of fizzing and a
colourless solution — this time containing **calcium ethanoate**:

2CH₃COOH(aq) + CaCO₃(s) → (CH₃COO)₂Ca(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

Notice that both equations need **two** acid molecules per
carbonate unit. The arithmetic is the metals section's again,
viewed from the other side: the carbonate ion is doubly charged
(CO₃²⁻), so it needs either two singly-charged metal ions or one
doubly-charged one — and it needs two protons to become water
and carbon dioxide. Each proton leaves behind one [[ethanoate-ion]]
in solution, so two protons means two CH₃COOH molecules on the
left. The salt side then just counts charges: two Na⁺ (each
with one ethanoate) or one Ca²⁺ (with two ethanoates).

This is also the reaction that makes the family's fizz a
diagnostic: any solution that fizzes on a carbonate and turns
limewater milky with the gas produced is behaving as an acid —
and for the carboxylic acids, gently. Ethanoic acid plus calcium
carbonate is, in fact, a household-scale example of acid-on-
limescale chemistry, run at vinegar strength rather than
laboratory strength.

:::key-point
Both of this chapter's salt families come from one move: the
ethanoate ion is 1−, so count the positive charge it must
neutralise. Metals: Mg²⁺ → (CH₃COO)₂Mg. Carbonates: CO₃²⁻ →
two protons, two ethanoates, and the salt holds whichever metal
the carbonate brought — CH₃COONa from sodium carbonate,
(CH₃COO)₂Ca from calcium carbonate. One counting rule, every
formula.
:::

:::exam-hint
The observation trio for a carbonate item is fizzing (carbon
dioxide gas), a colourless solution forming (the ethanoate salt
is soluble), and the limewater test turning milky if you route
the gas through it. Naming the salt scores separately from
describing the observation — write both. And the 2 in front of
CH₃COOH is not decorative: it is the carbonate's two negative
charges demanding two protons, and items ask for balanced
equations with the coefficient in place.
:::

:::misconception
"The carbon dioxide is part of the salt." The CO₂ escapes as a
gas — the fizz is the visual proof. The salt is only the ions
left dissolved in the solution: metal cation plus ethanoate
anion. Writing CO₂ into a salt formula (CH₃COONa·CO₂ and the
like) double-counts the carbonate's atoms; the carbonate ion
split into CO₂ and H₂O, and its metal joined the ethanoate.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write both carbonate equations — sodium and calcium —
balanced, with state symbols? Can you explain why two acid
molecules are needed per carbonate either through the CO₃²⁻
charge or through the two protons? Can you name both salts from
their ion pairs? Then 4.36C is fully delivered and only the
question bank remains.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 27 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete [[carboxylic-acid]] story. The family
is defined by the carboxyl group –COOH (4.34C); its four named
members up to four carbons come with the three-level formula
discipline and the count-them-all naming rule (4.35C); as
[[weak-acid]]s they react with metals and metal carbonates —
slower than the strong acids, leaving [[ethanoate-ion]] salts
and running the same charge arithmetic every time (4.36C); and
[[vinegar]], the everyday solution of [[ethanoic-acid]], is the
family's flagship (4.37C). Three equations anchor the chapter:
the magnesium reaction, the sodium carbonate reaction and the
calcium carbonate reaction.

Every specification statement of this chapter — 4.34C to 4.37C —
has been taught, and each now joins the platform question bank
through the links below, with practice items keyed to exactly
those statements.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's
core moves. Can you draw the carboxyl group with both bonds
explicit? Can you produce molecular, structural and displayed
levels for the four named acids? Can you write any metal
ethanoate or hydrogen-carbonate product from ion charges alone?
Can you explain the weak-acid rate difference through
dissociation? Any wobble is a section to revisit, not a reason
to start over.

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Drawing
and naming items open the set: structural formulae for named
acids, [[displayed-formula]] drawings with the COOH bonding
explicit, and naming from condensed structures. Identification items follow:
a drawn structure to be tested against a tick-table of the
alkene, alcohol and carboxylic-acid groups — read the drawing
bond by bond, because a molecule can legitimately tick two
boxes at once. A long oxidation item then reaches back to the
alcohols lesson: propan-1-ol heated under reflux with potassium
dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid, asking for the product's
full displayed formula (the oxidation lands on this chapter's
family), the orange-to-green colour change, a hazard critique of
an unsafe apparatus choice, and then the product tested in two
test-tubes — one with magnesium ribbon, one with sodium
carbonate solution — so both of this chapter's reaction families
run inside a single item. A finishing item balances the
vinegar-plus-sodium-hydrogencarbonate frame (a salt plus carbon
dioxide plus water) and asks for the reaction type and the
observation. The shapes are the chapter; the acid names are
just costumes.

:::exam-hint
Two habits pay in this bank. In equation items, the ethanoate
ion is always 1− — subscript the metal after the charges are
counted, and the coefficient of CH₃COOH follows the same count.
In explanation items, dissociation is the argument: weak means
partially ionised, lower H⁺ concentration, slower reaction —
"it is a weak acid so it is slower" without the mechanism earns
one mark where the dissociation sentence earns both.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards memorising these printed answers."
It rewards the transferable routines: the count-them-all naming
decode, the three-level formula ladder, the charge-first salt
arithmetic, the dissociation argument for rate differences. The
same skills re-ask through propanoic acid instead of ethanoic,
sodium carbonate instead of calcium, a drawn alcohol instead of
a drawn acid. Run the method and the costume does not matter.
:::

:::summary
- **The functional group (4.34C)**: carboxylic acids contain
  –COOH — carbonyl C=O and hydroxyl O–H on the same end carbon;
  built by oxidising the corresponding alcohol (microbial or
  dichromate(VI) routes).
- **Drawing and naming (4.35C)**: methanoic HCOOH (CH₂O₂),
  ethanoic CH₃COOH (C₂H₄O₂), propanoic CH₃CH₂COOH (C₃H₆O₂),
  butanoic CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (C₄H₈O₂); count total carbons including
  the –COOH carbon; no locant is ever needed; displayed formulae
  show the C=O and O–H explicitly.
- **Weak-acid behaviour (4.36C)**: pH about 3–5, blue litmus to
  red, partial dissociation (about 1 in 75 molecules) — slower
  than strong acids at equal concentration because the H⁺
  concentration is lower.
- **With metals**: salt + hydrogen —
  Mg(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → (CH₃COO)₂Mg(aq) + H₂(g); sodium
  dangerously reactive, zinc slower, below-hydrogen metals not
  at all; zinc ethanoate (CH₃COO)₂Zn.
- **With carbonates**: salt + carbon dioxide + water —
  Na₂CO₃(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → 2CH₃COONa(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) and
  2CH₃COOH(aq) + CaCO₃(s) → (CH₃COO)₂Ca(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l);
  two protons per carbonate ion.
- **Vinegar (4.37C)**: an aqueous solution containing ethanoic
  acid — the family's everyday representative.
:::

:::can-you
- write and draw the carboxyl group, and explain why it sits at
  the end of the chain?
- produce all three formula levels for the four named acids and
  explain the count-them-all naming rule?
- state the pH band and litmus result, and explain "weak" through
  partial dissociation with the 1-in-75 picture?
- write the magnesium equation with state symbols and build any
  metal ethanoate from ion charges?
- write both carbonate equations and explain the two-proton
  arithmetic?
- define vinegar chemically and place it inside the family?
:::

:::quick-check
If every line of the Can-you checklist above is a confident yes,
you are exam-ready on 4.34C–4.37C and the platform bank below is
pure consolidation. If any line wobbled, the fix is surgical:
jump back to that section, reread the key-point box, and retry
the equation — every section in this lesson was built so that a
single weak link can be re-forged without redoing the family.
:::
